Use this page once your main analysis runs and you want to know how much the
estimate depends on the choices you made. It covers changing one choice at a
time, and two design checks for confounding you cannot measure. You need your
main model from [Regression](regression.qmd), [Time-to-event](time-to-event.qmd)
or [Rates and rate ratios](rates-poisson.qmd); when you are done you have a set
of supplementary estimates to report next to it.

Register data lacks important lifestyle variables (smoking, BMI, alcohol, diet),
so reviewers will ask how robust your result is. A
**sensitivity analysis** repeats the main analysis under a different but
plausible assumption and checks whether the conclusion holds. If it holds, the
result stands stronger; if it collapses, you know a particular assumption is
carrying the result, and you should be honest about that.

Two principles: **pre-specify** your sensitivity analyses in the analysis plan
(otherwise they look like fishing for a nice number), and **report them
alongside** the main estimate, not instead of it.

*Variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own.* You
rarely need new packages here: a sensitivity analysis is usually your main
model run again with one changed choice.

## Robustness checks: change one choice at a time

Most sensitivity analyses consist of changing one choice at a time and
seeing whether the conclusion moves:

<div class="table-responsive">
<table class="table">
<thead>
<tr><th>What you vary</th><th>Why</th><th>Example</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Exposure definition</td><td>Are you capturing real use or just one incidental purchase?</td><td>Require <strong>2 filled prescriptions</strong> instead of 1</td></tr>
<tr><td>Outcome definition</td><td>Strict vs. broad capture of the outcome</td><td>Only <strong>primary diagnosis</strong> vs. also secondary diagnoses</td></tr>
<tr><td>Adjustment set</td><td>Does a single uncertain covariate carry the result?</td><td>Minimal vs. full adjustment; with/without a variable you are unsure is a confounder or a mediator</td></tr>
<tr><td>Restriction / lag time</td><td>Reduce reverse causation and protopathic bias (early symptoms of a not yet diagnosed outcome lead to the exposure)</td><td>Start follow-up <strong>6-12 months</strong> after index, so both the early events and the person-time before the lag are left out</td></tr>
<tr><td>Missing data</td><td>Does the estimate hold without the imputation assumptions?</td><td><strong>Complete-case</strong> vs. <strong>multiple imputation</strong> (see <a href="missing-data.qmd">Missing data</a>)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Censoring / follow-up</td><td>Is dropout informative?</td><td>Alternative censoring rule, or <strong>IPCW</strong> (weighting against selective dropout, see <a href="weighting-iptw.qmd">IP weighting</a>)</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>

The conclusion need not be *numerically identical* across the analyses - it just
has to **point the same way**. A hazard ratio moving from 1.8 to 1.6 is robust;
one shifting from 1.8 to 0.9 means the changed choice is carrying the result.

## Probe for unmeasured confounding

The checks above vary your **choices**. But register data also lacks variables
you do not have at all (smoking, BMI, etc.). Two design checks are widely
used against that kind of unmeasured confounding: a negative control outcome
can reveal it, and an active comparator can reduce it.

### Negative control outcome

**Idea:** pick an extra outcome the exposure **cannot possibly cause**, but
which is hit by the **same hidden confounders** as your real outcome. Run your
main model on it. If you still find an "effect", that is a **warning flag**: the
groups are systematically different (*residual confounding*, i.e. confounding
left after adjustment), and your main result is probably coloured by it too. If
the estimate instead sits close to 1, it supports your main analysis, but it
cannot rule out confounding that affects only your real outcome.

**Example (healthy-vaccinee bias).** Studies often find that
influenza-vaccinated older adults have markedly **lower all-cause mortality**.
But if you look at mortality **outside the influenza season** - a negative
control outcome, because the vaccine cannot protect against influenza when there
is no influenza - they are *still* "protected". That reveals the vaccinated are
healthier and more resourceful to begin with (*healthy-vaccinee bias*), not that
the vaccine itself lowers all-cause mortality that much. Jackson and
colleagues ran this check, as described by Lipsitch et al. (see Read more).

```r
library(survival) # coxph(), Surv()

# Main analysis: the effect on the REAL outcome
coxph(Surv(time_days, outcome) ~ exposure + age + sex, data = df)

# Negative control outcome: the EXACT same model, but an outcome the exposure cannot affect
# (here e.g.: death outside the influenza season). A clear "effect" here = a confounding warning.
# It needs its OWN follow-up: time_nco and nco_event are built exactly like time_days and
# outcome in Phase 12 (joins.qmd#follow-up-time), but with the NCO date in place of event_date.
coxph(Surv(time_nco, nco_event) ~ exposure + age + sex, data = df)
```

### Active comparator (new user)

**Idea:** instead of comparing drug users with **non-users** (who are wildly
different - they do not even have the indication), compare them with **new users
of an alternative drug for the same condition**. Both groups then share the
indication, so *confounding by indication* is sharply reduced. "New user" means
both start treatment at index, so you do not mix newly started and long-term
users (*prevalent-user bias*).

**Example.** You study whether glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists
(glucose-lowering drugs for type 2 diabetes, usually added to metformin) affect the risk of an outcome. If you
compare against **non-users**, you are really comparing people with and without
treatment-requiring diabetes - two wildly different groups, where the disease
itself confounds the picture. If you instead compare against new users of
dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors (another add-on drug for the same condition), the
groups are far more alike on indication and disease severity, and the estimate
is less coloured by *why* people are on treatment.

Active comparator is about how you build the cohort ([Phase 10 - Build your
study population](build-study-population.qmd)) - see the
new-user and risk-set logic in [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd).

::: {.callout-note}
**Self-controlled designs** (where the person is their own control and all
*time-invariant* confounding disappears) are a related approach in
register research. See [Self-controlled and family-based
designs](special-designs.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Read more"}

- Lund, Richardson & Stürmer, "[The Active Comparator, New User Study Design in
  Pharmacoepidemiology](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40471-015-0053-5)",
  *Curr Epidemiol Rep* 2015 - active comparator and new-user design.
- Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen & Cohen, "[Negative controls: a tool for detecting

  studies](https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0b013e3181d61eeb)", *Epidemiology* 2010 -
